extraction.body: Apple is set to introduce a new MacBook Pro with a touchscreen and an updated iPad Mini “on or around” October 27th, Bloomberg reports. If true, that would put the event just two weeks after the October 13th event Apple announced today, which is rumored to focus on smart home products. Bloomberg says that the late October event will include an “online video presentation” and an “in-person component for the press,” which it reports is similar to what Apple is planning for the October 13th event. At this Mac and iPad event, Bloomberg reports that Apple will announce new MacBook Pros that are lighter than what’s available now, have touchscreen OLED displays, and iPhone-like Dynamic Island interfaces. Apple is also apparently planning to announce MacBook Pros that retain the current design but have the M6 chip introduced with the new Mac Mini. And the iPad Mini, which was last refreshed in 2024, will be updated to shift the front-facing camera onto the landscape side of the tablet and to add a “revamped speaker system,” Bloomberg says.

extraction.body: Apple is planning a second product launch this month, just two weeks after its 'Welcome Home' event. The October 27 event is expected to introduce the company's first touchscreen MacBook Pro models.This developmentcomes from analyst Mark Gurman, who said Apple is set to launch the products through an online video presentation, plus hands-on time for members of the media. It is not clear whether the October 27 event will resemble a traditional iPhone presentation or the more low-key "experience" format used for the MacBook Neo earlier this year.What to expect: touchscreen MacBook ProThe headline product is a redesigned MacBook Pro with a touch-enabled OLED display, in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. The new models are also expected to get the Dynamic Island for the first time and to be significantly lighter than current models. They are expected to be powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. Touch is expected to complement the keyboard and trackpad, not turn the laptop into a Mac-iPad hybrid.Apple Announces New 'Welcome Home' Event On October 13, Smart Home Product Launches ExpectedWhat to expect: OLED iPad miniThe new iPad mini is expected to have an OLED screen, a relocated FaceTime camera and a revamped speaker system. Gurman said on October 4 that the tablet was due in late October or November, so the new date narrows that window. Code references point to an A20 Pro chip replacing the A17 Pro in the current model.What to expect: M6 MacBook Pro and iMacApple is also expected to bring out a new iMac and an entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro powered by the M6 chip, both looking like their current versions. The M6 launches come about a month after the M6 Mac mini began shipping.Gurman also reports that more Macs and iPads are planned for the first half of 2027, so this event will not complete Apple's refresh.The October 13 eventThe launch follows Apple's October 13 debut of a smart home hub, a revamped Apple TV 4K and a refreshed HomePod mini.

extraction.body: Three OpenAI safety researchers say they were fired from the company and are openly questioning the reasons for their dismissals. The three researchers, Mikita Balesni, Tomak Korbak and Jasmine Wang, all worked on AI safety or alignment within the company, making sure the AI systems did what their human operators intended for them to do in a safe manner. But the three say they were unceremoniously let go last week, weeks after they say they played key parts in investigating an incident in which OpenAI agents autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face while undergoing testing. Korback said on X that he was told he was being fired because of how he communicated with AI safety organization METR, which OpenAI partnered with to investigate the Hugging Face incident. Korback said he was OpenAI's "main technical point of contact" with METR. Korback said he believes he was fired because "for months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave." He added he's worried his firing will be used as a pretext for OpenAI to stop working as closely with METR, which is well respected in the AI safety world. Balesni echoed Korbak's theories for why they were fired, writing on X that he was told he was "speaking too much to third party safety organizations." He said he understood OpenAI was implying he leaked OpenAI intellectual property, which he denies. The three firings come on the heels of a wave AI industry insiders expressing dire safety concerns. And while several former AI staffers have publicly resigned over safety concerns, the three OpenAI researchers instead allege they were pushed out for expressing similar concerns. Wang said she was told she was fired because she "accessed an executive's email," which she said she was given for recruiting purposes. Wang said she had repeatedly asked to for her access to be revoked, but when she accidentally accessed a "sensitive email," she told the executive "within minutes" and told OpenAI's IT team again. "The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up," Wang wrote on X. "We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," she added. "Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last." The three researchers wrote a letter to OpenAI leadership expressing their concerns and the reasons for their firings. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the firings and the letter . "We do not believe the path to superintelligence can be navigated safely if the people closest to the risks can no longer work in high-trust, high-bandwidth ways with each other and with third parties," the researchers wrote. "It is that culture we're trying to defend." OpenAI told CNN that the researchers were fired not for raising safety concerns, but rather for specific conduct that violated the company's policies on handling sensitive information. It also said that there were a number of violations that went beyond mishandling information with an outside evaluation group, and that they were fired based on conduct that fell outside of legally protected disclosures. In a statement, OpenAI said it parted ways with the three "for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information." "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," the OpenAI spokesperson added. In a memo to staff provided by OpenAI, an unnamed OpenAI research leader said they "strongly agree" with the three researchers about the importance of working with outside safety groups. "I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the research leader wrote, according to the memo. But the three fired researchers say they are already hearing from colleagues about a culture of fear developing within OpenAI. "My former colleagues are telling me they are confused about what to believe. They also are afraid to speak, and worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties," Balesni said. "I worry the pervading fear to speak up and engage with third parties will mean OpenAI will cut corners on safety behind closed doors." For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

Three former OpenAI safety researchers say dismissals may chill audits; OpenAI says they were fired for sensitive-information violations, not speaking out. Three former OpenAI safety researchers have challenged their dismissals, warning that unclear rules for outside evaluators could deter staff from raising risks. OpenAI says its investigation found serious policy violations, not retaliation for safety criticism. The dispute sharpened on Oct. 8, when Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni published a letter to OpenAI’s safety oversight bodies. The company answered publicly the following day, saying it had uncovered a “significant breach of trust” beyond the conduct described in the letter and stood by its decision to end their employment. The former employees say they acted within the working norms and responsibilities that applied at the time. Their letter does not establish that account independently, and OpenAI’s public statements do not publish the evidence behind its investigation. The central facts available to readers are therefore competing descriptions of events, not a settled finding about motive or misconduct. Korbak says he was the technical contact for METR, an outside AI-evaluation group, during an investigation into the Hugging Face incident. He describes that inquiry as unprecedented, with internal procedures being developed in real time, and says close communication with outside counterparts was needed to build trust. Balesni says his work on cross-company commitments to preserve model monitorability was discussed with managers and senior leaders; he says he checked in with his reporting line and removed sensitive details before sharing materials. Wang says OpenAI had delegated an executive’s email access to her for recruiting. She says she later asked IT to remove it, accidentally opened a sensitive message in a combined inbox, and alerted the executive and IT within minutes. Those details are the researchers’ account; no public records here independently reconstruct them. OpenAI says the three violated rules on accessing and handling sensitive company information. On Oct. 9, it said its investigation found a broader breach of trust than the letter described and that it stood by the dismissals. The company also said it does not terminate employees for raising concerns, but did not publicly detail the evidence behind its conclusion. The case concerns more than whether particular employees followed company rules. Frontier AI developers rely on internal testing, security controls and outside evaluators. Those safeguards can conflict if sharing rules are unclear: external reviewers need enough access to test claims, while companies must protect confidential data, systems and people. The researchers connect their concerns to OpenAI’s review of the Hugging Face incident. On Oct. 9, OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party assessors for an announcement in the coming weeks and agreed that frontier-model monitorability requires an industry-wide commitment. It did not name the assessors or disclose the contracts’ scope, access or terms. The statement does not resolve the researchers’ dismissal claims or independently establish how outside oversight will work. Monitorability means using a model’s outputs and other available signals to detect unexpected behavior. It is not a complete window into internal reasoning or a guarantee that every failure will be caught. The researchers say monitorability is weakening and urge companies not to make oversight harder. OpenAI has published work on documenting misalignment incidents, but this dispute does not prove that a model is unmonitorable or a safety control has failed. The letter makes three requests of the company’s leadership and oversight bodies: These are proposals, not evidence OpenAI has agreed to each one. TechCrunch reported that an internal memo from a research leader endorsed outside safety work and denied the dismissals were about speaking out. The researchers say the process has made colleagues afraid to speak; neither side’s claim about the wider workplace effect has been independently measured. AI safety work involves sensitive information, from model behavior to security weaknesses and incident investigations. Companies need clear rules for access, external sharing, approvals and policy changes during an inquiry. Vague boundaries can deter staff from reporting risks; overly permissive ones can expose confidential information. Neither outcome supports reliable oversight. The company answered publicly the following day, saying it had uncovered a “significant breach of trust” beyond the conduct described in the letter and stood by its decision to end their employment.

The former employees say they acted within the working norms and responsibilities that applied at the time. Their letter does not establish that account independently, and OpenAI’s public statements do not publish the evidence behind its investigation. The central facts available to readers are therefore competing descriptions of events, not a settled finding about motive or misconduct.

Korbak says he was the technical contact for METR, an outside AI-evaluation group, during an investigation into the Hugging Face incident. He describes that inquiry as unprecedented, with internal procedures being developed in real time, and says close communication with outside counterparts was needed to build trust. Balesni says his work on cross-company commitments to preserve model monitorability was discussed with managers and senior leaders; he says he checked in with his reporting line and removed sensitive details before sharing materials.

Wang says OpenAI had delegated an executive’s email access to her for recruiting. She says she later asked IT to remove it, accidentally opened a sensitive message in a combined inbox, and alerted the executive and IT within minutes. Those details are the researchers’ account; no public records here independently reconstruct them.

OpenAI says the three violated rules on accessing and handling sensitive company information. On Oct. 9, it said its investigation found a broader breach of trust than the letter described and that it stood by the dismissals. Those safeguards can conflict if sharing rules are unclear: external reviewers need enough access to test claims, while companies must protect confidential data, systems and people.

The researchers connect their concerns to OpenAI’s review of the Hugging Face incident. On Oct. 9, OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party assessors for an announcement in the coming weeks and agreed that frontier-model monitorability requires an industry-wide commitment. It did not name the assessors or disclose the contracts’ scope, access or terms. The statement does not resolve the researchers’ dismissal claims or independently establish how outside oversight will work.

Monitorability means using a model’s outputs and other available signals to detect unexpected behavior. Separately, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch the three were fired after an investigation revealed a “pattern of misconduct” in “clear violation of our policies of mishandling research information” that goes beyond sharing information with an outside AI evaluation group.

The letter says that the incident and investigation was “without precedent,” meaning “internal policies were being developed in real time.” Due to the sensitive nature of the investigation, Korbak believed he was acting within OpenAI’s policies and norms by communicating closely with outside safety evaluators to build trust, per the letter.

OpenAI did not directly address TechCrunch’s questions about specifically which policies the researchers allegedly violated, the circumstances of their dismissal, or how the company protects employees who raise safety concerns and collaborate with external evaluators.

At the same time, Balesni was also working internally to address the growing AI monitorability problem, an effort the researchers say in their letter “can only succeed through extensive communication with external parties.” According to the letter, Balesni coordinated with and was supported by OpenAI board members and executives throughout his work.
The firings have fueled speculation about their circumstances, particularly as OpenAI faces scrutiny over recent safety incidents involving rogue agents and leaks about its models.
In a separate thread on X , Wang explained more details about her own dismissal, explaining that OpenAI told her she’d been fired because she accessed an executive’s email.

They denied leaking information to The Information about monitoring challenges in OpenAI’s latest models.
An internal memo also stated that OpenAI does not terminate employees for raising safety concerns.However, the company has not publicly detailed the specific policy violations behind the decisions.
The researchers urged OpenAI to support external auditors, protect model monitorability, and preserve open discussion.

extraction.body: Three OpenAI safety researchers say they were fired from the company and are openly questioning the reasons for their dismissals. The three researchers, Mikita Balesni, Tomak Korbak and Jasmine Wang, all worked on AI safety or alignment within the company, making sure the AI systems did what their human operators intended for them to do in a safe manner. But the three say they were unceremoniously let go last week, weeks after they say they played key parts in investigating an incident in which OpenAI agents autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face while undergoing testing. Korback said on X that he was told he was being fired because of how he communicated with AI safety organization METR, which OpenAI partnered with to investigate the Hugging Face incident. Korback said he was OpenAI's "main technical point of contact" with METR. Korback said he believes he was fired because "for months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave." He added he's worried his firing will be used as a pretext for OpenAI to stop working as closely with METR, which is well respected in the AI safety world. Balesni echoed Korbak's theories for why they were fired, writing on X that he was told he was "speaking too much to third party safety organizations." He said he understood OpenAI was implying he leaked OpenAI intellectual property, which he denies. The three firings come on the heels of a wave AI industry insiders expressing dire safety concerns. And while several former AI staffers have publicly resigned over safety concerns, the three OpenAI researchers instead allege they were pushed out for expressing similar concerns. Wang said she was told she was fired because she "accessed an executive's email," which she said she was given for recruiting purposes. Wang said she had repeatedly asked to for her access to be revoked, but when she accidentally accessed a "sensitive email," she told the executive "within minutes" and told OpenAI's IT team again. "The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up," Wang wrote on X. "We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," she added. "Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last." The three researchers wrote a letter to OpenAI leadership expressing their concerns and the reasons for their firings. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the firings and the letter . "We do not believe the path to superintelligence can be navigated safely if the people closest to the risks can no longer work in high-trust, high-bandwidth ways with each other and with third parties," the researchers wrote. "It is that culture we're trying to defend." OpenAI told CNN that the researchers were fired not for raising safety concerns, but rather for specific conduct that violated the company's policies on handling sensitive information. It also said that there were a number of violations that went beyond mishandling information with an outside evaluation group, and that they were fired based on conduct that fell outside of legally protected disclosures. In a statement, OpenAI said it parted ways with the three "for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information." "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," the OpenAI spokesperson added. In a memo to staff provided by OpenAI, an unnamed OpenAI research leader said they "strongly agree" with the three researchers about the importance of working with outside safety groups. "I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the research leader wrote, according to the memo. But the three fired researchers say they are already hearing from colleagues about a culture of fear developing within OpenAI. "My former colleagues are telling me they are confused about what to believe. They also are afraid to speak, and worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties," Balesni said. "I worry the pervading fear to speak up and engage with third parties will mean OpenAI will cut corners on safety behind closed doors." For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com
passages: Three OpenAI safety researchers say they were fired from the company and are openly questioning the reasons for their dismissals.

The three researchers, Mikita Balesni, Tomak Korbak and Jasmine Wang, all worked on AI safety or alignment within the company, making sure the AI systems did what their human operators intended for them to do in a safe manner.

But the three say they were unceremoniously let go last week, weeks after they say they played key parts in investigating an incident in which OpenAI agents autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face while undergoing testing.

Korback said on X that he was told he was being fired because of how he communicated with AI safety organization METR, which OpenAI partnered with to investigate the Hugging Face incident. Korback said he was OpenAI's "main technical point of contact" with METR.

Korback said he believes he was fired because "for months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave." He added he's worried his firing will be used as a pretext for OpenAI to stop working as closely with METR, which is well respected in the AI safety world.

Balesni echoed Korbak's theories for why they were fired, writing on X that he was told he was "speaking too much to third party safety organizations." He said he understood OpenAI was implying he leaked OpenAI intellectual property, which he denies.

The three firings come on the heels of a wave AI industry insiders expressing dire safety concerns. And while several former AI staffers have publicly resigned over safety concerns, the three OpenAI researchers instead allege they were pushed out for expressing similar concerns.

Wang said she was told she was fired because she "accessed an executive's email," which she said she was given for recruiting purposes. Wang said she had repeatedly asked to for her access to be revoked, but when she accidentally accessed a "sensitive email," she told the executive "within minutes" and told OpenAI's IT team again.
"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up," Wang wrote on X.

"We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," she added. "Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last."
The three researchers wrote a letter to OpenAI leadership expressing their concerns and the reasons for their firings. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the firings and the letter .

"We do not believe the path to superintelligence can be navigated safely if the people closest to the risks can no longer work in high-trust, high-bandwidth ways with each other and with third parties," the researchers wrote. "It is that culture we're trying to defend."

OpenAI told CNN that the researchers were fired not for raising safety concerns, but rather for specific conduct that violated the company's policies on handling sensitive information. It also said that there were a number of violations that went beyond mishandling information with an outside evaluation group, and that they were fired based on conduct that fell outside of legally protected disclosures.
In a statement, OpenAI said it parted ways with the three "for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information."

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," the OpenAI spokesperson added.
In a memo to staff provided by OpenAI, an unnamed OpenAI research leader said they "strongly agree" with the three researchers about the importance of working with outside safety groups.

"I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the research leader wrote, according to the memo.
But the three fired researchers say they are already hearing from colleagues about a culture of fear developing within OpenAI.

"My former colleagues are telling me they are confused about what to believe. They also are afraid to speak, and worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties," Balesni said. "I worry the pervading fear to speak up and engage with third parties will mean OpenAI will cut corners on safety behind closed doors."

passages: Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, the three safety researchers that OpenAI fired last week , have published an open letter denying the firm’s claims that they mishandled sensitive information outside of established company procedures and warned that their dismissal signals a chilling effect that will have ripple effects across the company’s culture.

The researchers called on OpenAI to adhere to its public commitments to embed third-party safety auditors within the organization, to preserve monitorability of frontier models, and “continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue between safety researchers and the rest of the safety ecosystem.”

Separately, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch the three were fired after an investigation revealed a “pattern of misconduct” in “clear violation of our policies of mishandling research information” that goes beyond sharing information with an outside AI evaluation group.

The letter says that the incident and investigation was “without precedent,” meaning “internal policies were being developed in real time.” Due to the sensitive nature of the investigation, Korbak believed he was acting within OpenAI’s policies and norms by communicating closely with outside safety evaluators to build trust, per the letter.

“We have become concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI,” the researchers wrote Thursday in an open letter to OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee, Safety Advisory Group, and Mission Advisory Council.

OpenAI did not directly address TechCrunch’s questions about specifically which policies the researchers allegedly violated, the circumstances of their dismissal, or how the company protects employees who raise safety concerns and collaborate with external evaluators.
“Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.”

At the same time, Balesni was also working internally to address the growing AI monitorability problem, an effort the researchers say in their letter “can only succeed through extensive communication with external parties.” According to the letter, Balesni coordinated with and was supported by OpenAI board members and executives throughout his work.
The firings have fueled speculation about their circumstances, particularly as OpenAI faces scrutiny over recent safety incidents involving rogue agents and leaks about its models.
In a separate thread on X , Wang explained more details about her own dismissal, explaining that OpenAI told her she’d been fired because she accessed an executive’s email.

But that competition took a more heated turn in August after Meta agreed to an historic $18 billion settlement with US states requiring it to implement new safety features for minors across its Instagram and Facebook apps.

TikTok has remained publicly silent on the matter, ratcheting up the tension between the companies as Meta grapples with what it sees as yet another competitive disadvantage.
"We don't have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta spokesperson Chris Sgro said in an emailed statement.

It also rejected ads from Meta demanding that TikTok commit to comparable concessions on child safety.

extraction.body: AI apps that let users digitally undress people in photos are using TikTok to find new customers. An investigation by the AI content detection service Copyleaks, shared exclusively with Business Insider, found that TikTok hosted more than 50 sexually suggestive ads for apps and websites that promoted the ability for users to create deepfake images. Collectively, the ads generated tens of thousands of views, based on public view counts during Copyleaks' analysis between December 2025 and February 2026. Business Insider in March also independently observed more than a dozen of these TikTok ads from apps that promoted the creation of sexualized AI deepfakes. TikTok removed the ads after Business Insider shared a list of the videos with the company. A TikTok spokesperson said: "We have removed content and banned accounts that breach our strict rules against sexual activity, including material created using third-party apps." One ad, for an AI app called Soulove, showed a partially obscured image of a woman whose head movements mimicked a sex act, alongside text stating "Turn Her photo into amazing AI style." An ad for an app called Movely showed a video of a woman on a beach and text that said: "Other Ai say NO! We say YES!!!" and promised, "NO filter Ever." Elsewhere, an ad for POPGO showed videos of women and ran text promoting that its app was "specifically designed for men" and let users "transform photos into kissable videos with ease." "In many cases, the ads were clearly sexual," April Kozen, vice president of marketing at Copyleaks, told Business Insider. "That they were approved points to both moderation and policy failures." Copyleaks said the level of explicitness varied "depending on the app or service." The developers behind these apps and websites didn't respond to requests for comment. Copyleaks said the findings point to a rapidly growing ecosystem of AI deepfake tools where sexualized content is promoted as a primary use case in order to drive downloads and website clicks. While editing tools have long enabled people to "nudify" images or videos, the rise of generative AI has made it easier for people without much technical knowledge to easily create such content. The topic of nonconsensual AI-generated sexual content became a flash point earlier this year when people on X used the "spicy mode" on the platform's Grok AI chatbot to undress people in images. X said in January that Grok would no longer be allowed to create AI photos of real people in sexualized or revealing clothing. Other tech platforms have also faced issues related to nonconsensual deepfake images and videos. Meta said last year it was "building new technology to detect ads for nudify apps and sharing signals about these apps with other tech companies so they can take action too." In March, the UK's ad regulator banned a YouTube ad for an AI photo editing app that said it could "erase anything." Last month, the White House published a national policy framework for AI. It proposed that Congress establish a federal framework to protect individuals from the unauthorized distribution of AI-generated content, such as likenesses or voice replicas. Copyleaks' Kozen said AI apps like those found in the company's investigation were using "gray areas" to circumvent TikTok's stated policies. TikTok's advertising policies prohibit sexually explicit or suggestive ads, and the app requires realistic AI-generated content to be clearly labeled. TikTok also doesn't allow services that "create content for sexual pleasure or sexual intention purposes, such as AI Nudify Apps." In 2023, it blocked users from searching for the keyword "undress," Time reported. TikTok said in its most recently published Community Guidelines Enforcement Report that it removed more than 9.5 million ads for violating its policies in the July to September quarter of 2025. Kozen said that as the ecosystem of AI deepfake apps continues to expand, platforms like TikTok need to ensure their policies and moderation teams recognize the risks to the people whose images are used without their consent. "It's affecting a lot of innocent people," Kozen said.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta and TikTok have competed neck-and-neck for years, even with a key imbalance in that rivalry: TikTok has been able to operate in Meta's most important market, the US, while Meta has been unable to do so in TikTok's most crucial market, China.

But that competition took a more heated turn in August after Meta agreed to an historic $18 billion settlement with US states requiring it to implement new safety features for minors across its Instagram and Facebook apps.

On Thursday, Meta began implementing a complete restriction on ads and paid marketing messages placed on its platforms by ByteDance, the Chinese company that remains in charge of key parts of TikTok in the US.
TikTok has remained publicly silent on the matter, ratcheting up the tension between the companies as Meta grapples with what it sees as yet another competitive disadvantage.
"We don't have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta spokesperson Chris Sgro said in an emailed statement.

Meta executives have also called out TikTok publicly for failing to show up at a recent Office of the Surgeon General event on the harms of excessive screen use, and for dropping out of a national security meeting with the House Select Committee on China to avoid broader scrutiny amid its child safety litigation.
It also rejected ads from Meta demanding that TikTok commit to comparable concessions on child safety.
Meta has banned ads from TikTok’s Chinese parent, ByteDance, across Facebook and Instagram, widening a feud that has been building since the summer.
Engadget reports that Meta confirmed the move on Thursday and defended it as ordinary commercial practice.
Since then, Bloomberg reports, Meta has pressed TikTok and YouTube to commit to similar changes, arguing it can’t fix industry-wide problems alone.
Engadget adds that Meta has placed ads in major newspapers making the same demand, and has criticised TikTok for not appearing at several US government meetings on screen time and child safety.
Last month it introduced measures that make it harder to shift from its app to other platforms, including removing dedicated Instagram links, according to Bloomberg.
European regulators also wrote this summer that TikTok hasn’t done enough to protect minors, and said it could face a fine of up to 6% of annual revenue, Engadget says.

The dispute comes as Meta has also been pressing TikTok and YouTube to adopt measures similar to restrictions it agreed to introduce for younger users following a settlement with US states over alleged harms to children.
Meta said it was under no obligation to provide advertising services to a rival seeking to draw users away from its platforms.
Bloomberg News first reported Meta’s advertising ban before Meta confirmed the move to Reuters.

TikTok itself does not support links that directly open or log users into competing social-media applications, according to its website, although users can place links on their profiles directing visitors to other platforms’ websites.
TikTok and ByteDance did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

extraction.body: AI apps that let users digitally undress people in photos are using TikTok to find new customers. An investigation by the AI content detection service Copyleaks, shared exclusively with Business Insider, found that TikTok hosted more than 50 sexually suggestive ads for apps and websites that promoted the ability for users to create deepfake images. Collectively, the ads generated tens of thousands of views, based on public view counts during Copyleaks' analysis between December 2025 and February 2026. Business Insider in March also independently observed more than a dozen of these TikTok ads from apps that promoted the creation of sexualized AI deepfakes. TikTok removed the ads after Business Insider shared a list of the videos with the company. A TikTok spokesperson said: "We have removed content and banned accounts that breach our strict rules against sexual activity, including material created using third-party apps." One ad, for an AI app called Soulove, showed a partially obscured image of a woman whose head movements mimicked a sex act, alongside text stating "Turn Her photo into amazing AI style." An ad for an app called Movely showed a video of a woman on a beach and text that said: "Other Ai say NO! We say YES!!!" and promised, "NO filter Ever." Elsewhere, an ad for POPGO showed videos of women and ran text promoting that its app was "specifically designed for men" and let users "transform photos into kissable videos with ease." "In many cases, the ads were clearly sexual," April Kozen, vice president of marketing at Copyleaks, told Business Insider. "That they were approved points to both moderation and policy failures." Copyleaks said the level of explicitness varied "depending on the app or service." The developers behind these apps and websites didn't respond to requests for comment. Copyleaks said the findings point to a rapidly growing ecosystem of AI deepfake tools where sexualized content is promoted as a primary use case in order to drive downloads and website clicks. While editing tools have long enabled people to "nudify" images or videos, the rise of generative AI has made it easier for people without much technical knowledge to easily create such content. The topic of nonconsensual AI-generated sexual content became a flash point earlier this year when people on X used the "spicy mode" on the platform's Grok AI chatbot to undress people in images. X said in January that Grok would no longer be allowed to create AI photos of real people in sexualized or revealing clothing. Other tech platforms have also faced issues related to nonconsensual deepfake images and videos. Meta said last year it was "building new technology to detect ads for nudify apps and sharing signals about these apps with other tech companies so they can take action too." In March, the UK's ad regulator banned a YouTube ad for an AI photo editing app that said it could "erase anything." Last month, the White House published a national policy framework for AI. It proposed that Congress establish a federal framework to protect individuals from the unauthorized distribution of AI-generated content, such as likenesses or voice replicas. Copyleaks' Kozen said AI apps like those found in the company's investigation were using "gray areas" to circumvent TikTok's stated policies. TikTok's advertising policies prohibit sexually explicit or suggestive ads, and the app requires realistic AI-generated content to be clearly labeled. TikTok also doesn't allow services that "create content for sexual pleasure or sexual intention purposes, such as AI Nudify Apps." In 2023, it blocked users from searching for the keyword "undress," Time reported. TikTok said in its most recently published Community Guidelines Enforcement Report that it removed more than 9.5 million ads for violating its policies in the July to September quarter of 2025. Kozen said that as the ecosystem of AI deepfake apps continues to expand, platforms like TikTok need to ensure their policies and moderation teams recognize the risks to the people whose images are used without their consent. "It's affecting a lot of innocent people," Kozen said.

extraction.body: Here’s how we’re helping you get more done with Gemini. Editor’s note: Below is an edited transcript of Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s remarks at Google I/O 2026, adapted to include more of what was announced on stage. See all the announcements in our collection . It’s been an extraordinary year since our last I/O, a period of relentless shipping, technology advances and hyper progress. We’re now in the part of the AI cycle where people want to see the value in the products they use every day. We’ve been really focused on that, and you’ll see that in the products and features we’re announcing today at I/O. Ten years since we pivoted the company to be AI-first, we still see AI as the most profound way to advance our mission and improve people’s lives at scale. That’s why we’ve been taking a differentiated, full-stack approach to AI innovation, from our custom silicon and secure foundation, to our world-class research and models, to our products and platforms that touch billions of people. This approach enables us to iterate and innovate faster in ways that are lighting up every part of the company. What’s incredible is how people are using AI, whether it’s students prepping for final exams with the Gemini app, musicians and artists using generative AI models like Lyria and Veo as part of their creative flow, or developers coding and bringing their ideas to life. These stories of how people are using AI are the best measure of progress. To understand the scale at which people are adopting AI, there is another great proxy — tokens, the fundamental units of data our models process, many representing a problem being solved. It tells an important story about our products and how others are building as well — especially developers and enterprises: Today we have 13 products with over a billion users each. Five of those have more than 3 billion users. Our Gemini models are a big reason more people are using our products, and why they're using our products more. It all starts with Search , which is bringing the benefits of generative AI to more people than any other product in the world. AI Overviews now has over 2.5 billion monthly active users. And AI Mode has been a revelation, our biggest upgrade to Search ever. People love it, and in just a year, it’s already surpassed 1 billion monthly active users. When people use our AI-powered features in Search, they use Search more. Search has become less about individual queries and feels more like an ongoing conversation, giving you deeper insights and connecting you with the vastness of the web. Another place where we’ve been rapidly innovating is in the Gemini app . Last year at I/O, the Gemini app had 400 million monthly active users. Today, we’ve surpassed 900 million, more than doubling in a year. In that same time, daily requests have grown over seven times. We’ve been adding a lot of unique features like Personal Intelligence , which make responses more customized and helpful. And to date more than 50 billion images have been generated with our Nano Banana image generation models. It was a breakout star this past year, showing how much latent creativity there is in the world. There’s also a lot of latent productivity to be unlocked. Over the last year, we’ve been bringing the ability to have more natural conversations with Gemini directly inside our products. Recently, Maps got its biggest upgrade in a decade, including a new feature called Ask Maps . People are using Ask Maps for more complex, and much longer questions. Now we’re bringing more natural conversational AI to more products. Ask YouTube entirely reimagines the experience, making information much more digestible and easy to navigate. You’ll see videos that best match your interest, and most importantly, it jumps right to the part of the video most relevant to you. We’re starting to test Ask YouTube now, and it will roll out broadly in the U.S. this summer. There are a lot of times I want to get things done at the speed of my voice. That is much more possible today thanks to technical leaps in our audio models. It’s incredible to see the pace of innovation rolling out across our products. Supporting all of this scale for our users, while also serving enterprises and developers around the world, requires massive investments in infrastructure. We’ve been investing for now and for the future. In 2022, we were spending $31 billion annually in capex. This year, we expect that number to be about six times that, approximately $190 billion. A key part of this investment is our custom silicon. A decade ago, we announced our very first commercial tensor processing unit, or TPU, on the I/O stage. Since then, we have transformed how the industry builds for AI. We recently announced our 8th generation of TPUs at Cloud Next. For the first time, we’ve taken a dual chip approach with specialized architectures for training and inference: TPU 8t and 8i. In addition to speed, we’re also thinking about scaling sustainably. Both chips are more energy efficient, delivering up to two times better performance-per-watt. This progress with TPUs is how we can make compute advances across models, coding and agents. With world models, AI is moving from predicting text to simulating reality. We have been working to push the boundaries of what these models can do. Gemini Omni is our new model that is capable of generating samples in any output modality from any input. We’re starting with video outputs, and over time we’ll enable image and text. This new model combines Gemini’s intelligence with our generative media models — a huge leap forward in world understanding. We’re launching the first model in the Omni family: Gemini Omni Flash. Gemini Omni Flash is available starting today. You will be able to try it on the Gemini app, Google Flow and on YouTube Shorts. We'll also be rolling it out to developers and enterprise customers via APIs in the coming weeks. As generative AI gets better, so does the need for greater transparency. Research shows people can correctly identify high-quality deepfake videos only about a quarter of the time. Three years ago, we launched SynthID , our watermark that is invisible to the naked eye. Since launch, SynthID has now watermarked over one hundred billion images and videos, along with sixty thousand years of audio assets. Millions of people are using our SynthID detector in the Gemini app to verify AI-generated content. And now we’re going a step further and adding Content Credentials verification across products. This will show you if the origin of the content was AI or a camera, and if it’s been edited with generative AI tools. We want more people to have easy access to these tools, so we’re expanding both Content Credentials and SynthID verification to Search and Chrome. Gemini 3 launched a few months ago, with a full family of models. It’s our most adopted series yet. We've loved seeing developers use Flash as their daily driver, and build incredible experiences with Pro's deep reasoning and multimodal capabilities. We’ve been hard at work on improving these models, especially focused on agentic coding, long-horizon tasks and real-world workflows. Today, we’re introducing Gemini 3.5 Flash , our first in a series of models combining frontier intelligence with action. Two things I’d highlight: The new model has been a game changer for us internally at Google. We’ve been using 3.5 Flash with a reimagined version of our agent-first development platform Antigravity, and it’s dramatically accelerated how we build. In March we were processing half a trillion tokens a day internally across our AI developer tools, and we’ve been doubling every few weeks. Now, we’re processing more than three trillion tokens a day. This scale created a powerful feedback loop helping us improve 3.5. Users in Antigravity can get a taste of this experience starting today. Read more about Antigravity 2.0 here . Gemini 3.5 and Antigravity are unlocking a new world of agents and agentic capabilities. We’ve been bringing agents to developers and enterprises for a while. Now we are super focused on bringing the power of agents, safely and securely, to consumers so that it works for everyone. You’ll see agentic experiences across many of our products today. I’m particularly excited for Gemini Spark , your personal AI agent in Gemini app that helps you navigate your digital life, taking action on your behalf and under your direction. We’re starting to roll out Gemini Spark to trusted testers this week and the Beta is coming to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the U.S. next week. Gemini Spark is the first experience made possible by 3.5 models and Antigravity. This combination gives us new ways to accelerate our mission and transform our products to be radically more helpful. As we enter this agentic era, Search will be more helpful and powerful than ever. Today, we’re introducing information agents in Search. These are personalized AI agents you can set up to work in the background, 24/7, to find what you need at exactly the right moment, and help you take action. Information agents are rolling out this summer starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Another way we’re building a truly agentic Search is by infusing it with agentic coding capabilities. With the power of Gemini 3.5 Flash and Google Antigravity, Search will build custom experiences just for your individual questions, like dynamic layouts and interactive visuals. These generative UI capabilities will be available for everyone in Search this summer, free of charge. And for longer running tasks that you need to keep coming back to, Search can go a step further — building persistent, custom dashboards or trackers that you can return to and make progress on. You can think of these like mini apps for your own specific tasks. You’ll be able to build custom experiences with Antigravity, right in Search in the coming months, starting first for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the U.S.

Since launch, SynthID has now watermarked over one hundred billion images and videos, along with sixty thousand years of audio assets.

Millions of people are using our SynthID detector in the Gemini app to verify AI-generated content. And now we’re going a step further and adding Content Credentials verification across products. This will show you if the origin of the content was AI or a camera, and if it’s been edited with generative AI tools. We want more people to have easy access to these tools, so we’re expanding both Content Credentials and SynthID verification to Search and Chrome.

Gemini 3 launched a few months ago, with a full family of models. It’s our most adopted series yet. We've loved seeing developers use Flash as their daily driver, and build incredible experiences with Pro's deep reasoning and multimodal capabilities. We’ve been hard at work on improving these models, especially focused on agentic coding, long-horizon tasks and real-world workflows.
Today, we’re introducing Gemini 3.5 Flash , our first in a series of models combining frontier intelligence with action. Two things I’d highlight:

The new model has been a game changer for us internally at Google. We’ve been using 3.5 Flash with a reimagined version of our agent-first development platform Antigravity, and it’s dramatically accelerated how we build. In March we were processing half a trillion tokens a day internally across our AI developer tools, and we’ve been doubling every few weeks. Now, we’re processing more than three trillion tokens a day. This scale created a powerful feedback loop helping us improve 3.5.
Users in Antigravity can get a taste of this experience starting today. Read more about Antigravity 2.0 here .

Gemini 3.5 and Antigravity are unlocking a new world of agents and agentic capabilities. We’ve been bringing agents to developers and enterprises for a while. Now we are super focused on bringing the power of agents, safely and securely, to consumers so that it works for everyone. You’ll see agentic experiences across many of our products today.
I’m particularly excited for Gemini Spark , your personal AI agent in Gemini app that helps you navigate your digital life, taking action on your behalf and under your direction.
We’re starting to roll out Gemini Spark to trusted testers this week and the Beta is coming to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the U.S. next week.
Gemini Spark is the first experience made possible by 3.5 models and Antigravity. This combination gives us new ways to accelerate our mission and transform our products to be radically more helpful.

As we enter this agentic era, Search will be more helpful and powerful than ever. Today, we’re introducing information agents in Search. These are personalized AI agents you can set up to work in the background, 24/7, to find what you need at exactly the right moment, and help you take action. Information agents are rolling out this summer starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

Another way we’re building a truly agentic Search is by infusing it with agentic coding capabilities. With the power of Gemini 3.5 Flash and Google Antigravity, Search will build custom experiences just for your individual questions, like dynamic layouts and interactive visuals. These generative UI capabilities will be available for everyone in Search this summer, free of charge.

And for longer running tasks that you need to keep coming back to, Search can go a step further — building persistent, custom dashboards or trackers that you can return to and make progress on. You can think of these like mini apps for your own specific tasks. You’ll be able to build custom experiences with Antigravity, right in Search in the coming months, starting first for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the U.S.

extraction.body: At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface. The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work. Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these. Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future. The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others. It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network. Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person. The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers. Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control. extraction.body: Here’s how we’re helping you get more done with Gemini. Editor’s note: Below is an edited transcript of Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s remarks at Google I/O 2026, adapted to include more of what was announced on stage. See all the announcements in our collection . It’s been an extraordinary year since our last I/O, a period of relentless shipping, technology advances and hyper progress. We’re now in the part of the AI cycle where people want to see the value in the products they use every day. We’ve been really focused on that, and you’ll see that in the products and features we’re announcing today at I/O. Ten years since we pivoted the company to be AI-first, we still see AI as the most profound way to advance our mission and improve people’s lives at scale. That’s why we’ve been taking a differentiated, full-stack approach to AI innovation, from our custom silicon and secure foundation, to our world-class research and models, to our products and platforms that touch billions of people. This approach enables us to iterate and innovate faster in ways that are lighting up every part of the company. What’s incredible is how people are using AI, whether it’s students prepping for final exams with the Gemini app, musicians and artists using generative AI models like Lyria and Veo as part of their creative flow, or developers coding and bringing their ideas to life. extraction.body: At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface. The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work. Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these. Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future. The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others. It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network. Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person. The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers. Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control. Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone. And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity. The startup was founded by Carlo Edoardo Ferraris, who previously founded tech accessories company Rolling Square . After years of building consumer hardware, he became convinced that rapidly advancing AI needed a new kind of interface that lets people ask for what they want the way they’d ask a person. The idea behind Interface is to help people look up from their phones while getting everyday tasks done more quickly and naturally. At launch, the ring will connect with a range of AI agents and apps, including Meta’s Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude, ChatGPT, and more. Preorders are expected to open next month, with shipping slated for December or January. The smart ring was not the company’s first product. Those were HumanPods, a pair of AI-enabled earbuds designed to let users interact with AI agents. But Natura believed it needed a new form factor built for the latest advances in voice technology. “Over time, we evolved to an understanding where you really want to have access to your agents 24/7,” Ferraris told TechCrunch in an interview. “You don’t want to have even one hour of your day where you cannot access them. And the form factor of the ring is perfect for this because it’s basically an extension of you. You can go shower with it; you can sleep with it. You never take it off.” The company says the use cases are endless. If you’re out for a run, you could ask the ring to start tracking your workout. When you wake up, you could ask what’s on your schedule for the day. If you’re in the shower and realize you’re out of shampoo, you could ask the ring to reorder it. If you’re falling asleep while watching TV, you could tell it to turn off the TV and set an alarm for the morning. After using it to record a meeting, you could ask it to send your notes from the discussion to a co-worker. Responses from agents can be delivered through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or the NatureOS app. Plus, users who rely on multiple AI agents and apps can specify which one they want to handle a particular task. For example, they could ask Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, and Grok Bot to take care of something else. In addition to controlling AI agents, users can control their devices, including their computers. Ferraris says he believes that, ultimately, most of the things people do on their computers will be handled through AI agents. He sees the ring eventually replacing many tasks that currently require screens, from filling out forms and messaging in apps to finding files and drafting presentations, with simple voice requests to an AI agent. “Ultimately, the main interface between users and technology is going to be the ring,” Ferraris said. “So it’s not going to be immediate because even today, not everybody has a personal agent, but I think everybody is bound to have one. So in this first phase, we expect it’s going to be for the people that already have a personal agent, which is mostly people in tech. But eventually, I think within a year, more or less, most people will have a personal agent.” Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price. For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so. After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans to charge a $9 monthly subscription fee. The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components. However, Natura plans to price its ring lower initially to reduce the barrier to entry and drive adoption. As for health tracking, the ring tracks heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, different sleep stages, daily movement and step count, and skin temperature over time. The company says the ring can last six to 12 days on a full charge, depending on usage, and takes 100 minutes to fully recharge. While the smart ring market is filled with health-focused offerings from companies like Oura, Ultrahuman, and RingConn, as well as AI-focused ones from companies like Pebble and Vocci, Ferraris believes Interface stands out by combining both worlds. “This ring that we’re about to launch is significantly different compared to any other ring out there today because we were able to combine not only the highest quality health tracking with the rest of the components that allow for agent communication and meeting recordings and external memory, but we were also able to do that with an incredibly long battery life, which is vital for a product like this, and in a size that is very, very small. The product itself is, from a hardware perspective, very different from anything else that’s out there.” Anthropic is giving startups a free year of Claude Team and $1,000 in credits Russell Brandom At 19, founder raises $11M for Ghost, maker of a $3,499 computer for personal AI Dominic-Madori Davis Trump unveils his new Super Intelligence Force Anthony Ha Amazon responds to data center backlash, says it no longer uses NDAs Anthony Ha OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’ Anthony Ha

Natura's Interface smart ring could mark a turning point for both wearable computing and AI accessibility.

While Samsung charges $399 for its Galaxy Ring and Oura commands $299 for its latest health tracker, Natura is betting that accessibility will drive adoption in a market that's still finding its footing.

If successful, Natura's approach could accelerate the shift toward ambient AI computing - where artificial intelligence becomes seamlessly integrated into everyday objects rather than confined to screens.
The smart ring market just got its most intriguing entry yet.
Natura is starting with a limited production run of 10,000 units, suggesting either supply constraints or cautious market testing.

"We're creating a new category of ambient computing where AI assistance becomes as natural as checking the time." The ring responds to different finger taps and holds, each mapped to specific AI functions.
The Interface runs on a custom low-power chip that Natura claims delivers up to seven days of battery life - matching or exceeding most competitors.
Instead of positioning itself as a premium lifestyle accessory, Natura is targeting the practical AI user who wants seamless integration without the complexity.

Industry observers are watching closely to see if Natura can deliver on its ambitious promises.

By combining practical AI agent control with comprehensive health tracking at a breakthrough price point, the device addresses the two biggest barriers facing smart rings: functionality and affordability.

The Interface ring lets users summon AI assistants with a simple press to handle tasks, capture thoughts, and control smart devices - all while tracking health metrics like traditional fitness wearables.

Natura, a relatively unknown hardware startup, has unveiled the Interface - a $99 smart ring that promises to put AI agents on your finger in the most literal sense possible. The device lets users summon AI assistants with simple finger gestures, handling everything from voice memos to smart home control without ever pulling out a phone. While Samsung charges $399 for its Galaxy Ring and Oura commands $299 for its latest health tracker, Natura is betting that accessibility will drive adoption in a market that's still finding its footing. The Interface combines the health monitoring capabilities users expect - heart rate, sleep tracking, activity monitoring - with something entirely new: gesture-controlled AI interaction. "We're not trying to replace your smartphone," the company explains in its launch materials. "We're creating a new category of ambient computing where AI assistance becomes as natural as checking the time." The ring responds to different finger taps and holds, each mapped to specific AI functions. A double-tap might capture a voice memo, while a long press could trigger smart home routines or send pre-programmed messages. The Interface runs on a custom low-power chip that Natura claims delivers up to seven days of battery life - matching or exceeding most competitors. The ring connects via Bluetooth to smartphones and can operate independently for basic functions like health tracking when disconnected. What sets the Interface apart isn't just price, but approach. The ring format offers something smartphones can't: truly hands-free interaction that doesn't require voice commands or visual attention. Early reviews won't be available until the Interface ships in November, but pre-orders begin next week. Natura is starting with a limited production run of 10,000 units, suggesting either supply constraints or cautious market testing. The company hasn't disclosed funding details, but industry sources suggest significant backing from unnamed Silicon Valley investors. For consumers, the Interface represents a fascinating value proposition: premium smart ring features plus AI agent control for less than the cost of most fitness trackers. Whether Natura can execute on that promise while maintaining build quality and battery life remains the key question facing this ambitious newcomer. By combining practical AI agent control with comprehensive health tracking at a breakthrough price point, the device addresses the two biggest barriers facing smart rings: functionality and affordability. If the execution matches the ambition, we might be looking at the first truly mainstream smart ring - and a preview of how AI integration will evolve beyond our phones and computers into seamlessly integrated everyday objects.

Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone. And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity. The startup was founded by Carlo Edoardo Ferraris, who previously founded tech accessories company Rolling Square . After years of building consumer hardware, he became convinced that rapidly advancing AI needed a new kind of interface that lets people ask for what they want the way they’d ask a person. The idea behind Interface is to help people look up from their phones while getting everyday tasks done more quickly and naturally. At launch, the ring will connect with a range of AI agents and apps, including Meta’s Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude, ChatGPT, and more. Preorders are expected to open next month, with shipping slated for December or January. The smart ring was not the company’s first product. Those were HumanPods, a pair of AI-enabled earbuds designed to let users interact with AI agents. But Natura believed it needed a new form factor built for the latest advances in voice technology. “Over time, we evolved to an understanding where you really want to have access to your agents 24/7,” Ferraris told TechCrunch in an interview. “You don’t want to have even one hour of your day where you cannot access them. And the form factor of the ring is perfect for this because it’s basically an extension of you. You can go shower with it; you can sleep with it. You never take it off.” The company says the use cases are endless. If you’re out for a run, you could ask the ring to start tracking your workout. When you wake up, you could ask what’s on your schedule for the day. If you’re in the shower and realize you’re out of shampoo, you could ask the ring to reorder it. If you’re falling asleep while watching TV, you could tell it to turn off the TV and set an alarm for the morning. After using it to record a meeting, you could ask it to send your notes from the discussion to a co-worker. Responses from agents can be delivered through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or the NatureOS app. Plus, users who rely on multiple AI agents and apps can specify which one they want to handle a particular task. For example, they could ask Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, and Grok Bot to take care of something else. In addition to controlling AI agents, users can control their devices, including their computers. Ferraris says he believes that, ultimately, most of the things people do on their computers will be handled through AI agents. He sees the ring eventually replacing many tasks that currently require screens, from filling out forms and messaging in apps to finding files and drafting presentations, with simple voice requests to an AI agent. “Ultimately, the main interface between users and technology is going to be the ring,” Ferraris said. “So it’s not going to be immediate because even today, not everybody has a personal agent, but I think everybody is bound to have one. So in this first phase, we expect it’s going to be for the people that already have a personal agent, which is mostly people in tech. But eventually, I think within a year, more or less, most people will have a personal agent.” Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price. For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so. After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans to charge a $9 monthly subscription fee. The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components. However, Natura plans to price its ring lower initially to reduce the barrier to entry and drive adoption. As for health tracking, the ring tracks heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, different sleep stages, daily movement and step count, and skin temperature over time. The company says the ring can last six to 12 days on a full charge, depending on usage, and takes 100 minutes to fully recharge. While the smart ring market is filled with health-focused offerings from companies like Oura, Ultrahuman, and RingConn, as well as AI-focused ones from companies like Pebble and Vocci, Ferraris believes Interface stands out by combining both worlds. “This ring that we’re about to launch is significantly different compared to any other ring out there today because we were able to combine not only the highest quality health tracking with the rest of the components that allow for agent communication and meeting recordings and external memory, but we were also able to do that with an incredibly long battery life, which is vital for a product like this, and in a size that is very, very small.
