HARRISBURG — Ahead of the Nov. 3 election, Pennsylvania voters have identified the economy as a top issue, driven by concerns about the cost of living, unemployment, and utility prices. It's a key focus in the 10th Congressional District race, a rematch between Republican incumbent Scott Perry , who's held the seat since 2013, and Democratic candidate Janelle Stelson , a former news anchor. It's also one of three toss-up U.S. House races in Pennsylvania identified by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report . The purple district covers the entirety of Dauphin County, including Harrisburg, in addition to portions of Cumberland and York Counties. Members of Congress, elected for two-year terms, vote on legislation that affects the economy, including changes to federal taxes and budgets, as well as government spending. They can also secure federal funding and advocate for the district they represent by shaping and voting for legislation. While Perry and Stelson differ on tariffs and the ongoing war in Iran, which have contributed to increases in the price of groceries and gas, they both support tax breaks and healthcare reform. The economic issue they align on most is employment, favoring pathways for skilled and technical trades. He also voted for President Donald Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," signed into law on July 4, 2025, which permanently extended most of the individual and business tax cuts from the TCJA that were set to expire at the end of that year. It also created federal income tax deductions for tips, overtime pay, and taxpayers 65 and older through 2028. Stelson has criticized his votes, arguing the cuts benefit corporations and wealthy earners instead of workers while increasing the national deficit. On her campaign website, she says she'll "support tax breaks for the hard working middle class, not billionaires." And in campaign materials reviewed by Spotlight PA, she pledges to support permanently not taxing tips and overtime pay. While the OBBA is expected to boost the economy in the short term, researchers at Brookings, a nonpartisan think tank, said in a preliminary analysis released in March that it will raise federal deficits by between $3.7 and $5.1 trillion over the next decade. The Trump administration's tariffs, a tax tacked on to imported goods, have been an ongoing point of disagreement between the campaigns. Stelson has said she'll work to repeal Trump's tariffs and advocate for a more stable foreign policy. Recently, Perry said Americans "need to be patient" for the promised benefits of Trump's tariff policies to play out while prices are high, citing long-term relief. Perry is also a co-sponsor of the FairTax Act of 2025 , introduced by U.S. Rep. Earl L. Carter (R., Ga.). If enacted, the law would eliminate the IRS and replace several federal taxes, including income, payroll, estate, and gift, with a sales tax beginning in 2027. So far, the legislation has only been introduced and has not yet seen a vote. Since those tax credits expired at the end of 2025, nearly 202,000 enrollees on PENNIE, the state health insurance exchange, have dropped their coverage. Stelson has called it a "crisis and a failure of leadership," and said that making sure healthcare is affordable and accessible is one of her top priorities , including by making ACA tax credits permanent. Perry's campaign website shows he supports healthcare reforms "to reduce costs, improve the quality of care and increase access to coverage," including expanding health savings accounts and allowing individuals to "purchase healthcare across state lines." The bipartisan federal housing law, which went into effect in July, aims to make housing more affordable by banning investors who own at least 350 houses from buying more, among other provisions. A proponent of limiting federal reach , Perry defended his vote by arguing the federal government has "meddled in the housing market for decades," which he says has led to less affordability for buyers. He also said he voted against it because of language in the legislation about the potential creation of a central bank digital currency, which he vehemently opposes. Stelson, who criticized Perry's vote, has offered a six-point affordable housing plan that includes building on the law by making home construction faster, easier, and cheaper; expanding small-dollar home loans; and voting to repeal tariffs she argues raise prices on lumber and drywall. Perry's campaign website does not include housing as an issue listed on his platform. The average price of a gallon of gas as of Sept. 14 in Pennsylvania is $4.50, according to AAA , higher than the $4.32 national average. This time last year, the average price of a gallon of gas was $3.25 in Harrisburg . Both Perry and Stelson have pointed to the war, stretching into its seventh month, as a catalyst for the rising cost of gas. Stelson has said the war needs to "go away," and that she'd vote to end the conflict. Perry, who supports the war, has said he hopes a resolution will soon be reached. Both Perry and Stelson have signaled their support for expanding and reforming job training outside of higher education. Stelson, who has described the commonwealth's minimum wage as "outrageous," has proposed concentrating more on vocational and technical training for mechanics, plumbers, electricians, woodworkers, and tradespeople in general in schools. Perry has focused more on skilled manufacturing , saying thousands of these jobs remain unfilled in central Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania's minimum wage has been $7.25 since the federal minimum went up in 2009, and has remained stagnant even as neighboring states' have increased. Last year, the Democratic-controlled state House voted to raise minimum wage to $15 an hour in 20 of its counties, and to $12 in the rest . Since then, HB 2189 has sat in the Republican-controlled Senate, awaiting a vote. extraction.body: Democrat Janelle Stelson holds a slight lead against Representative Scott Perry for a House seat in Pennsylvania's 10th Congressional District, new polling shows. According to polling from the leading super PAC supporting House Democrats in next year's midterms shared with Politico Playbook , Stelson, a former local TV anchor, is 3 percentage points ahead of Perry in a head-to-head matchup. Newsweek has contacted the House Majority PAC for comment. Perry, former chair of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, has represented the district since 2019. He may be in danger of losing his seat to Stelson, who narrowly lost to him by just over 5,000 votes in November. The survey from the House Majority PAC, conducted July 10-11, asked: "If the candidates for Congress next time were Democrat Janelle Stelson and Republican Scott Perry, who would you vote for?" The poll found 46 percent of likely voters said they would vote for Stelson, while 43 percent backed Perry. Eleven percent were undecided. The survey also measured voter sentiment toward both candidates. When asked whether they held a favorable or unfavorable opinion of Stelson, 35 percent said they viewed her favorably, while 33 percent had an unfavorable view. Thirty-two percent said they were unsure. Meanwhile, 49 percent of respondents said they disapproved of Perry's job performance, while 36 percent expressed approval and 16 percent were undecided. "Today I'm announcing my Congressional campaign against Scott Perry. He just voted for the biggest Medicaid cuts in history, to pay for billionaire tax breaks. This week, WITF News is publishing stories highlighting Republican Congressman Scott Perry’s and Democratic challenger Janelle Stelson’s responses to questions about the issues facing voters in Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District. The Nov. 3 race is a rematch between Perry, who has held the seat since 2013, and Stelson, a former TV news anchor. The race is considered a “toss-up” by Cook Political Report , along with two other U.S. House races in Pennsylvania. The 10th Congressional District covers all of Dauphin County and parts of Cumberland and York counties. WITF News is presenting the candidates’ responses as they were provided to us, without altering their answers. The responses are presented so voters can compare how the two candidates speak about issues that affect people in the 10th District. Candidates were asked the following five questions about technology and AI. Perry submitted one response addressing the section as a whole, while Stelson responded to each question individually. “ AI has the potential to be a gamechanger in so many areas, from energy to healthcare innovation. But like any new technology, it must be developed responsibly. The same goes for the development of data centers. Decisions about development are and should be made at the local level, and guardrails should be put in place to ensure that development occurs responsibly – and not at the expense of Citizens, ratepayers, and landowners. We’re in a race against China on AI that we must win – period. Whoever dominates AI will dominate the planet and we cannot live as subjects under Chinese rule. That doesn’t’ mean, however, that every data center is linked to national security interests. We should have transparency of and control over our data and how associated data centers are using it. For example, if the data center being proposed next to your housing development is just being used to market more products for your local box store – NO. If it’s trying to addict our kids (and others) to online sites – adult and otherwise – also NO. Leaving this powerful new technology to antisocial tech billionaires who decide what it is and how it’s to be used is unacceptable. The last thing we need to do is mirror Governor Shapiro’s actions of offering tax credits to some of the wealthiest companies on the planet who have not the slightest allegiance to America.” I want to invest in the future of our economy and make sure we create the jobs of the future right here in Pennsylvania. We need to incentivize innovation and manufacturing here in America to make sure technological breakthroughs and job creation happens here at home, not overseas. That said, Congressman Perry voted to give tens of billions in new tax breaks to build more data centers. He said we cannot “afford to slow down the buildout” of more data centers. I oppose those tax breaks and believe we can’t afford to let homeowners pay higher electric and water bills because of these data centers. AI should enhance our work, not replace our work. I support creating a regulatory framework that places humans at the center of progress. And as the job landscape changes, we need to be investing in concrete pathways to good-paying jobs across sectors, including more plans for high-quality jobs that do not require a 4-year college degree. HARRISBURG — Ahead of the Nov. 3 election, Pennsylvania voters have identified the economy as a top issue, driven by concerns about the cost of living, unemployment, and utility prices. It's a key focus in the 10th Congressional District race, a rematch between Republican incumbent Scott Perry , who's held the seat since 2013, and Democratic candidate Janelle Stelson , a former news anchor. It's also one of three toss-up U.S. House races in Pennsylvania identified by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report . The purple district covers the entirety of Dauphin County, including Harrisburg, in addition to portions of Cumberland and York Counties. Members of Congress, elected for two-year terms, vote on legislation that affects the economy, including changes to federal taxes and budgets, as well as government spending. They can also secure federal funding and advocate for the district they represent by shaping and voting for legislation. While Perry and Stelson differ on tariffs and the ongoing war in Iran, which have contributed to increases in the price of groceries and gas, they both support tax breaks and healthcare reform. The economic issue they align on most is employment, favoring pathways for skilled and technical trades. He also voted for President Donald Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," signed into law on July 4, 2025, which permanently extended most of the individual and business tax cuts from the TCJA that were set to expire at the end of that year. It also created federal income tax deductions for tips, overtime pay, and taxpayers 65 and older through 2028. Stelson has criticized his votes, arguing the cuts benefit corporations and wealthy earners instead of workers while increasing the national deficit. On her campaign website, she says she'll "support tax breaks for the hard working middle class, not billionaires." And in campaign materials reviewed by Spotlight PA, she pledges to support permanently not taxing tips and overtime pay. While the OBBA is expected to boost the economy in the short term, researchers at Brookings, a nonpartisan think tank, said in a preliminary analysis released in March that it will raise federal deficits by between $3.7 and $5.1 trillion over the next decade. The Trump administration's tariffs, a tax tacked on to imported goods, have been an ongoing point of disagreement between the campaigns. Stelson has said she'll work to repeal Trump's tariffs and advocate for a more stable foreign policy. Recently, Perry said Americans "need to be patient" for the promised benefits of Trump's tariff policies to play out while prices are high, citing long-term relief. Perry is also a co-sponsor of the FairTax Act of 2025 , introduced by U.S. Rep. Earl L. Carter (R., Ga.). If enacted, the law would eliminate the IRS and replace several federal taxes, including income, payroll, estate, and gift, with a sales tax beginning in 2027. So far, the legislation has only been introduced and has not yet seen a vote. Since those tax credits expired at the end of 2025, nearly 202,000 enrollees on PENNIE, the state health insurance exchange, have dropped their coverage. Stelson has called it a "crisis and a failure of leadership," and said that making sure healthcare is affordable and accessible is one of her top priorities , including by making ACA tax credits permanent. Perry's campaign website shows he supports healthcare reforms "to reduce costs, improve the quality of care and increase access to coverage," including expanding health savings accounts and allowing individuals to "purchase healthcare across state lines." The bipartisan federal housing law, which went into effect in July, aims to make housing more affordable by banning investors who own at least 350 houses from buying more, among other provisions. A proponent of limiting federal reach , Perry defended his vote by arguing the federal government has "meddled in the housing market for decades," which he says has led to less affordability for buyers. He also said he voted against it because of language in the legislation about the potential creation of a central bank digital currency, which he vehemently opposes. Stelson, who criticized Perry's vote, has offered a six-point affordable housing plan that includes building on the law by making home construction faster, easier, and cheaper; expanding small-dollar home loans; and voting to repeal tariffs she argues raise prices on lumber and drywall. Perry's campaign website does not include housing as an issue listed on his platform. The average price of a gallon of gas as of Sept. 14 in Pennsylvania is $4.50, according to AAA , higher than the $4.32 national average. This time last year, the average price of a gallon of gas was $3.25 in Harrisburg . Both Perry and Stelson have pointed to the war, stretching into its seventh month, as a catalyst for the rising cost of gas. Stelson has said the war needs to "go away," and that she'd vote to end the conflict. Perry, who supports the war, has said he hopes a resolution will soon be reached. Both Perry and Stelson have signaled their support for expanding and reforming job training outside of higher education. Stelson, who has described the commonwealth's minimum wage as "outrageous," has proposed concentrating more on vocational and technical training for mechanics, plumbers, electricians, woodworkers, and tradespeople in general in schools. Perry has focused more on skilled manufacturing , saying thousands of these jobs remain unfilled in central Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania's minimum wage has been $7.25 since the federal minimum went up in 2009, and has remained stagnant even as neighboring states' have increased. Last year, the Democratic-controlled state House voted to raise minimum wage to $15 an hour in 20 of its counties, and to $12 in the rest . Since then, HB 2189 has sat in the Republican-controlled Senate, awaiting a vote. extraction.body: Democrat Janelle Stelson holds a slight lead against Representative Scott Perry for a House seat in Pennsylvania's 10th Congressional District, new polling shows. According to polling from the leading super PAC supporting House Democrats in next year's midterms shared with Politico Playbook , Stelson, a former local TV anchor, is 3 percentage points ahead of Perry in a head-to-head matchup. Newsweek has contacted the House Majority PAC for comment. Perry, former chair of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, has represented the district since 2019. He may be in danger of losing his seat to Stelson, who narrowly lost to him by just over 5,000 votes in November. The survey from the House Majority PAC, conducted July 10-11, asked: "If the candidates for Congress next time were Democrat Janelle Stelson and Republican Scott Perry, who would you vote for?" The poll found 46 percent of likely voters said they would vote for Stelson, while 43 percent backed Perry. Eleven percent were undecided. The survey also measured voter sentiment toward both candidates. When asked whether they held a favorable or unfavorable opinion of Stelson, 35 percent said they viewed her favorably, while 33 percent had an unfavorable view. Thirty-two percent said they were unsure. Meanwhile, 49 percent of respondents said they disapproved of Perry's job performance, while 36 percent expressed approval and 16 percent were undecided. "Today I'm announcing my Congressional campaign against Scott Perry. He just voted for the biggest Medicaid cuts in history, to pay for billionaire tax breaks. We deserve better than a career politician who keeps selling us out," Stelson said in a statement on X, formerly Twitter , on Monday. Janelle Stelson, in a statement announcing her congressional bid: "Scott Perry has spent more than a decade in DC taking votes that hurt us instead of delivering results – and he just sold us out again by casting the deciding vote for the largest Medicaid cuts in history, all to fund more tax cuts for billionaires. "People around here are sick and tired of career politicians like Scott Perry betraying them at every turn. I'm running to give Central Pennsylvanians the voice they deserve and to fight to lower costs, protect Social Security and Medicare, ensure a woman's right to choose and secure the border." National Republican Congressional Committee's (NRCC) spokeswoman Maureen O'Toole, in a statement on Monday : "Welcome back to certified loser Janelle Stelson! If there's one thing we know for sure, it's that Janelle Stelson, who won't even bother to live in the district she wants to represent, doesn't stand a chance against Scott Perry. Pennsylvanians have rejected her before, and they'll gladly do so again in 2026."

passages: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died.
In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project.
A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.
And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.
Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959.
Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article.
In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News. Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said. She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.” “She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.” Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death. passages: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90.

Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible.

“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.

“She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.”

Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”

“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said.
She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.”
“She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.”
Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

The trailblazing pioneer played a crucial role in the development of flight software for NASA's Apollo Program, which was responsible for taking humans to the moon for the first time. Hamilton was an integral part of NASA's Apollo program, which landed human beings on the moon for the first time in 1969. Hamilton was a computer scientist who led the Software Engineering Division of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory, which contracted with NASA to develop the Apollo program's computers onboard flight software, according to NASA. Hamilton initially joined MIT in 1959 as a weather prediction software writer. She then joined Project Apollo and by 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. Because of her work on the Apollo program during this time, Hamilton is credited with kickstarting the concept of software engineering and coining the term, which is so widespread and referenced today.Hamilton has published over 130 publications and eventually became a successful computing entrepreneur and CEO, according to MIT News.She received many accolades, awards, honors, and recognition for her life's work. One of the most prominent awards Hamilton received was the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Hamilton was given the medal by President Barack Obama in 2016. Obama said at the time, "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon." She also was granted the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for her scientific and technical contributions.Hamilton has connections throughout the Midwest. Her family then moved to Michigan's Upper Peninsula and Hamilton graduated from Hancock High School. Hamilton then attended the University of Michigan before transferring to Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, about an hour east of Indianapolis, right on the Indiana-Ohio border. She earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958 before moving to Boston in 1959, where she soon found her footing at MIT. Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn. "To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved," Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics told MIT News."Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers. Hers was a career dedicated to preventing errors and what she called ‘handling the unknown,’" says de Weck. "She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from."

She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at MIT and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. And a Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. She graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News. Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama. Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90.

Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible.

“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at MIT and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

In recent years a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. And a Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.

She graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”

“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

passages: Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. Hamilton was a computer scientist who led the Software Engineering Division of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory, which contracted with NASA to develop the Apollo program's computers onboard flight software, according to NASA. Hamilton initially joined MIT in 1959 as a weather prediction software writer. She then joined Project Apollo and by 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. Because of her work on the Apollo program during this time, Hamilton is credited with kickstarting the concept of software engineering and coining the term, which is so widespread and referenced today.Hamilton has published over 130 publications and eventually became a successful computing entrepreneur and CEO, according to MIT News.She received many accolades, awards, honors, and recognition for her life's work. One of the most prominent awards Hamilton received was the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Hamilton was given the medal by President Barack Obama in 2016. Obama said at the time, "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon." She also was granted the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for her scientific and technical contributions.Hamilton has connections throughout the Midwest. Her family then moved to Michigan's Upper Peninsula and Hamilton graduated from Hancock High School. Hamilton then attended the University of Michigan before transferring to Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, about an hour east of Indianapolis, right on the Indiana-Ohio border. She earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958 before moving to Boston in 1959, where she soon found her footing at MIT. Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn. "To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved," Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics told MIT News."Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers. Hers was a career dedicated to preventing errors and what she called ‘handling the unknown,’" says de Weck. "She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from."

Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90.

Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible.

“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at MIT and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

In recent years a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. And a Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.

She graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”

“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

The president’s statement came days after he officially renamed ‘Artificial Intelligence’ to ‘Super Intelligence.’ The Press Office of California’s Governor also criticized the president’s post. sources.title: Donald Trump Orders White House To Label AI Critics Enemies, Demands “Superintelligence” Term - NewsCord
passages: President Donald Trump said on October 8 via his Truth Social account that the White House regards anyone who uses the term “artificial intelligence (AI)” instead of “superintelligence (SI)” as an enemy.

Trump’s September 29 executive order required federal departments and agencies “to the maximum extent permitted by law” to use “‘Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, public communications, websites,” among other official communications.
Donald Trump created the Superintelligence to coordinate the United States’ policy on AI
The BBC reported that demand for “.si” domain names surged after the executive order, with 44,000 websites with the “.si” ending registered in September.
Trump’s rebranding also drew criticism in the New Scientist piece, which quoted Trump saying, “The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake, and it is not fake.”
Trump also attended the “New Golden Age Summit” at the Donald J.
Trump Peace Institute (USIP) in Washington, D.C., where he unveiled a $6 billion (approximately 8 trillion Korean won) investment and support plan for science and technology.
Elon Musk said on X that SpaceX would rename its AI unit, SpaceXAI, to SpaceXSI, and Business Insider reported that SpaceXAI’s X account still said “SpaceXAI” as of Thursday afternoon.
Donald Trump claims he will rename AI to 'more accurate' term 'super intelligence'
By executive decree, Trump renames Artificial Intelligence as 'Superintelligence'
Trump’s warning about AI: he will consider those who do not speak of "superintelligence" as enemies.
Trump Announces Creation of "Superintelligence Task Force" to Coordinate US Government AI Efforts

extraction.body: President Donald Trump said on Thursday that anyone who doesn't use his preferred term of super intelligence (SI) will be considered an "enemy" of the White House. "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump's statement suggests the White House may punish companies or individuals who do not abide by its preferred speech, which would be a potential textbook First Amendment violation if enforced. The White House has moved to rebrand artificial intelligence, which Trump said suggests that the technology is "fake." While some companies, most notably Meta, which has a SuperIntelligence Labs, had super intelligence embedded in their branding before Trump's recent move, their descriptions were more about the future of artificial intelligence than an outright rejection of the terminology itself. After meeting with industry leaders in late September at the White House, Trump signed an executive order that required federal departments and agencies "to the maximum extent permitted by law" to use "'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, public communications, websites," among other official communications. The order did not apply to private-sector companies like OpenAI because the White House has no legal authority to enforce such a measure. Since Trump's statements and orders, at least one company has followed the White House's wishes. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that the space and technology company would rename its AI unit, SpaceXAI, to SpaceXSI. If Musk follows through on his promise, it would be the second such rebrand for what was originally known as xAI this year. In February, SpaceX announced that it was acquiring xAI, makers of the Grok chatbot, and rechristened the unit as SpaceXAI in July. As of Thursday afternoon, SpaceXAI's X account still said "SpaceXAI." It remains to be seen what other leading AI and tech companies will do. There was a bit of awkwardness after Trump made his wishes known on the same day of the highly anticipated AI lunch. During a White House panel discussion, Nvidia CEO Jensen Wang corrected himself when he said "AI" instead of "SI." In comments made with Trump standing just feet from him, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said the company "builds artificial intelligence" to help everyone. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently dismissed the possibility of renaming the company during an interview with Politico. "No plans to do that," he told the Politico Decoded podcast. "But we have been talking about super intelligence a lot and we will continue to talk about it."

extraction.body: President Donald Trump said on Thursday that anyone who doesn't use his preferred term of super intelligence (SI) will be considered an "enemy" of the White House. "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump's statement suggests the White House may punish companies or individuals who do not abide by its preferred speech, which would be a potential textbook First Amendment violation if enforced. The White House has moved to rebrand artificial intelligence, which Trump said suggests that the technology is "fake." While some companies, most notably Meta, which has a SuperIntelligence Labs, had super intelligence embedded in their branding before Trump's recent move, their descriptions were more about the future of artificial intelligence than an outright rejection of the terminology itself. After meeting with industry leaders in late September at the White House, Trump signed an executive order that required federal departments and agencies "to the maximum extent permitted by law" to use "'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, public communications, websites," among other official communications. The order did not apply to private-sector companies like OpenAI because the White House has no legal authority to enforce such a measure. Since Trump's statements and orders, at least one company has followed the White House's wishes. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that the space and technology company would rename its AI unit, SpaceXAI, to SpaceXSI. If Musk follows through on his promise, it would be the second such rebrand for what was originally known as xAI this year. In February, SpaceX announced that it was acquiring xAI, makers of the Grok chatbot, and rechristened the unit as SpaceXAI in July. As of Thursday afternoon, SpaceXAI's X account still said "SpaceXAI." It remains to be seen what other leading AI and tech companies will do. There was a bit of awkwardness after Trump made his wishes known on the same day of the highly anticipated AI lunch. During a White House panel discussion, Nvidia CEO Jensen Wang corrected himself when he said "AI" instead of "SI." In comments made with Trump standing just feet from him, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said the company "builds artificial intelligence" to help everyone. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently dismissed the possibility of renaming the company during an interview with Politico. "No plans to do that," he told the Politico Decoded podcast. "But we have been talking about super intelligence a lot and we will continue to talk about it."

extraction.body: Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90. Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering". Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September. "To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division. It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon. "I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring. The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved. But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT. The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her. Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969 In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel. At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space". Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958. She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree. From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts. "We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media. "Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Hamilton being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then President Barack Obama in 2016

extraction.body: MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90. In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist. She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity. “I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency. Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended. “It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said. Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. “Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

extraction.body: Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90. Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering". Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September. "To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division. It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon. "I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring. The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved. But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT. The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her. Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969 In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel. At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space". Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958. She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree. From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts. "We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media. "Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Hamilton being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then President Barack Obama in 2016

Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended. “It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project.

She also proposed a software fix to prevent the error happening during a real mission, but she was overruled on the grounds that the highly trained astronauts were never going to make that same mistake.
Yet during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, that’s exactly what happened: Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during the flight, causing the on-flight navigational data to vanish.
Hamilton and her team were called in to solve the error, and after that her proposed changes were integrated into the program.

A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline.

In 2015, the Apollo software she helped to develop was added in its entirety to the code-sharing site GitHub.

And in 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure after a set originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock, honoring her and several other women of NASA history, became available worldwide.
By 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software.

“From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 .
We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s.
Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.
Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust.
Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
Hamilton continued to work at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s.
“Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful,” says Jerry M.
Wohletz SM ’97, PhD ’00, president and CEO at Draper.
“Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers.
Hers was a career dedicated to preventing errors and what she called ‘handling the unknown,’” says de Weck.
“She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from.”
During this time, Hamilton began to take an interest in software reliability — a new and largely unexplored concept at the time.

A decade later, Hamilton founded another software company, Hamilton Technologies, “to provide products and services to modernize the planning, system engineering and software development process in order to maximize reliability, lower cost and accelerate time to market.”
Hamilton created a program add-on in the technical documentation warning users not to launch P01 during flight.

Hamilton Technologies’ flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language and methodology for engineering complex software systems that prioritize error prevention and defensive programming.

extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, a profoundly influential computer scientist best known for leading the software engineering team at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab during NASA’s Apollo program, died on Sep. 30. She was 90. A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline. She worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, after which she became a successful computing entrepreneur and CEO. Her life’s work was recognized with many awards and honors, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama, whose citation noted: “Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon.” “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” says Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Margaret Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success. And for her that was just the beginning! She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.” Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton began studying mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958. She moved to Boston, Massachusetts, in 1959 with her husband while he pursued a law degree. Hamilton soon found a temporary position in the meteorology department at MIT, working with professor of meteorology Edward N. Lorenz SM ’43, ScD ’48 on weather prediction software. This was her first entry point into computer programming, and her work would go on to inform Lorenz’s future publications on chaos theory. From there, Hamilton took a role as a programmer at MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1961, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States’ first air defense system. Hamilton wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer (XD-1), used by the U.S. Air Force to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this time, Hamilton began to take an interest in software reliability — a new and largely unexplored concept at the time. In 1965 Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw an advertisement in the newspaper: The Instrumentation Lab at MIT was seeking people to develop software to “send man to the moon.” The lab had won the contract from NASA to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project. Hamilton worked first on the software for the uncrewed Apollo missions and then was promoted into leading the team developing the on-board flight software for the crewed missions. By 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software. “From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 . “There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s. Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure. Dedication and commitment were a given. Mutual respect was across the board. Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” “Defensive” programming and priority-driven software take humans to the moon Hamilton discovered a talent for leadership, as well as a keen instinct for problem-solving and critical thinking that would prove to save Project Apollo several times over. There was the incident that became known as “the Lauren error”: One day, her daughter Lauren, then four years old, was playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab when she somehow activated a pre-launch program, called P01, while the simulator was in midflight — which crashed the simulator altogether. Hamilton created a program add-on in the technical documentation warning users not to launch P01 during flight. She also proposed a software fix to prevent the error happening during a real mission, but she was overruled on the grounds that the highly trained astronauts were never going to make that same mistake. Yet during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, that’s exactly what happened: Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during the flight, causing the on-flight navigational data to vanish. Hamilton and her team were called in to solve the error, and after that her proposed changes were integrated into the program. This was an early example of “defensive” programming, the practice of building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own. Hamilton’s most famous contribution to the Apollo program came during the pivotal Apollo 11 mission to land on the moon in July of 1969. Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised the alarm. It had detected a 1202 error: The computer was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch, and it was possible the system would not be able to handle the complex landing procedure. But Hamilton and her team had engineered priority-driven software, able to shut down unnecessary background tasks in order to prioritize mission-critical tasks. Houston trusted Hamilton’s software and allowed the mission to proceed, and two men walked on the moon for the first time. Hamilton continued to work at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s. As the Apollo program wound down, the Instrumentation Lab spun out of MIT to become the independent Draper Laboratory . “Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful,” says Jerry M. Wohletz SM ’97, PhD ’00, president and CEO at Draper. “Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.” Hamilton went on to create her first software company, Higher Order Software, in 1976. The firm was based on Hamilton’s software engineering approach of error prevention and fault tolerance. A decade later, Hamilton founded another software company, Hamilton Technologies, “to provide products and services to modernize the planning, system engineering and software development process in order to maximize reliability, lower cost and accelerate time to market.” Hamilton Technologies’ flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language and methodology for engineering complex software systems that prioritize error prevention and defensive programming. Throughout her career, Hamilton worked to achieve recognition for software engineering as a dedicated discipline. “I fought to bring the software legitimacy so that it — and those building it — would be given its due respect, and thus I began to use the term ‘software engineering’ to distinguish it from hardware and other kinds of engineering, yet treat each type of engineering as part of the overall systems engineering process,” Hamilton told El Pais in 2018 . “When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing. It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas. Software eventually and necessarily gained the same respect as any other discipline.” Among her many awards and honors, Hamilton was recognized with the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for scientific and technical contributions in 2003; the Computer History Museum Fellow Award in 2017; the Intrepid Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019; and induction into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2022. Later in life, Hamilton become an icon for women in science and technology, especially after a now-famous photo, showing her next to a printout of her MIT team’s Apollo code, began circulating online. In 2015, the Apollo software she helped to develop was added in its entirety to the code-sharing site GitHub. And in 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure after a set originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock, honoring her and several other women of NASA history, became available worldwide. “Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers. Hers was a career dedicated to preventing errors and what she called ‘handling the unknown,’” says de Weck. “She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from.” Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; four great grandchildren; and her siblings John, David, and Kathryn. A memorial service will take place in the spring in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering “priority-driven software” to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important, according to MIT as quoted by BBC.

MIT News also said Hamilton worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and later founded two software companies, and ABC News said she was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, including through a Lego set unveiled in 2017 that included a figure of Hamilton.
Margaret Hamilton, a profoundly influential computer scientist best known for leading the software engineering team at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab during NASA’s Apollo program, died on Sep.
“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement.
She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.”
Intrigued by the challenge, Hamilton applied, and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project.

She also proposed a software fix to prevent the error happening during a real mission, but she was overruled on the grounds that the highly trained astronauts were never going to make that same mistake.
Yet during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, that’s exactly what happened: Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during the flight, causing the on-flight navigational data to vanish.
Hamilton and her team were called in to solve the error, and after that her proposed changes were integrated into the program.
This was an early example of “defensive” programming, the practice of building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own.
Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised the alarm.
It had detected a 1202 error: The computer was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch, and it was possible the system would not be able to handle the complex landing procedure.
A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline.

Later in life, Hamilton become an icon for women in science and technology, especially after a now-famous photo, showing her next to a printout of her MIT team’s Apollo code, began circulating online.
In 2015, the Apollo software she helped to develop was added in its entirety to the code-sharing site GitHub.

And in 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure after a set originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock, honoring her and several other women of NASA history, became available worldwide.
By 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software.

“From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 .
